title: The conservationist who’s building bridges between bats and people
text:
The conservationist who’s building bridges between bats and people
For decades, Merlin Tuttle has been a leading advocate for bats.
Merlin Tuttle recalls entering his first bat cave almost seven decades ago, as a teenager living in Tennessee. Leaving behind a beautiful spring afternoon, he went into the cold, dark chamber and soon noticed small movements. He turned his light in that direction, and a colony of gray bats suddenly awakened, flapping their wings and squeaking.
He barely flinched. “It just never occurred to me to be frightened,” he says.
That teenager became Dr. Tuttle, one of the world’s leading voices for bat conservation. Born in Hawaii and raised west of Knoxville, he has traveled the world studying and advocating for the maligned mammals. Forty years ago, he chose Austin, Texas, as his home – and the headquarters for his nonprofit work – after he discovered that a colony of bats had roosted there, too.
Debunking fears
Austin is a living tribute to how a city can learn to love bats. Thanks in large part to Dr. Tuttle’s efforts, the city overcame its fear of the furry, fanged flyers and is now home to the largest urban bat colony in North America.
In 1980, the Texas Department of Transportation renovated the Congress Avenue bridge in the city’s downtown. The project added
concrete beams that, it transpired, are an ideal artificial habitat for Mexican free-tailed bats. Within a few years, tens of thousands of the animals were roosting under the bridge during the summer months.
Austin, Texas, is a living tribute to how a city can learn to love bats. Thanks in large part to Merlin Tuttle’s efforts, the city overcame its fear of the furry, fanged flyers and is now home to the largest urban bat colony in North America.
Initially, Austinites were not very welcoming.
“Bat colonies sink teeth into city,” read one local newspaper headline in 1984.
In a television report two years earlier, the city’s health director had said little to ease residents’ concerns.
“How much rabies there would be in this bat population, I don’t know,” the official said. “It’s something we have to look into.”
Dr. Tuttle has devoted his career to debunking the fears popularly associated with bats.
He points out that bats can carry rabies, but only a small percentage of wild bats are infected. (The incidence of rabies in bats is lower than in other mammals, such as raccoons, foxes, cats, and dogs.)
On the positive side, bats serve as natural pest control by eating vast quantities of insects. They also pollinate plants and crops, and enrich soil with their droppings, known as guano.
Dr. Tuttle’s challenge is that the bad press about bats has had a long head start on the good press.
As early as 1897, Bram Stoker’s fictional vampire Dracula could transform into a bat. The image of bloodthirsty nocturnal flyers beating their leathery wings has been a constant in popular culture ever since. The fact that bats typically nest in dark, out-of-the-way places doesn’t help, either. Photographs of bats often show them in gloved hands, or flying through dark skies, fangs bared.
Thus, one of the most potent tools in Dr. Tuttle’s long conservation career has been his photography. He has spent decades perfecting how to find, observe, and handle bats in a way that makes them look both beautiful and nonthreatening in photographs.
“Back in the ’80s, you looked at every single picture of a bat, [and] all you saw was teeth,” says Bert Grantges, a friend of Dr. Tuttle’s who has accompanied him on research trips around the world. “In Merlin’s photos ... they weren’t scary.”
Photography, he adds, has been “a critical piece to [Dr. Tuttle] creating a relatable story to an unrelatable animal.”
A source of pride
Dr. Tuttle had developed an interest in small mammals years before he entered the bat cave as a teen.
Before he graduated from high school, he had presented research to the Smithsonian Institution about the migratory patterns of the bats near his house. Before he received a bachelor’s degree in zoology from Andrews University in Michigan, the Smithsonian had offered him the opportunity to co-direct an expedition to Venezuela to study mammals in the Amazon. He went on to obtain his master’s degree and Ph.D. from the University of Kansas, before settling into a job as a curator at a museum in Milwaukee.
By 1986, he had brought his newly formed nonprofit, Bat Conservation International (BCI), to Austin, where the bats under the Congress Avenue bridge were being threatened with nets, blowtorches, and even cyanide gas.
Over the years, however, Austinites have come to view the colony of bats under the bridge with pride instead of alarm. The bats there now number about 1.5 million.
Every summer, tourists flock to the bridge at dusk to watch bats pour out from under the bridge for their nightly insect hunt. The spectacle attracts 140,000 people – and about $10 million – to the city every year, according to the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department. The bats also save the state’s agriculture industry about $1.4 billion each year in pest control costs.
On one warm August evening in Austin, almost 200 people are gathered at the Congress Avenue bridge. The city’s glass skyline has turned orange against the setting sun, and the rustling and squeaking of bats are audible.
At the front of the crowd, Natalie and Steve Keene – visiting from the United Kingdom – are back for the second night in a row. The previous evening, 45% of the colony had emerged, an app had told them.
“I’d never seen anything like that before in the world,” says Mrs. Keene.
A few minutes later, under a darkening sky, a gasp ripples through the crowd. Bats pour out from the bridge, carving a black “S” into the air. The crowd looks up, smiling in awe.
“An incredible advocate”
Under Dr. Tuttle’s leadership, BCI bought land surrounding a bat cave north of San Antonio. Bracken Cave, as it’s known, is now home to the world’s largest bat colony, housing more than 15 million Mexican free-tailed bats during the summer. In the ’90s, Dr. Tuttle also helped design an artificial bat cave on a private preserve west of Austin that is now home to more than 200,000 Mexican free-tailed bats, according to Texas Parks and Wildlife. He left BCI in 2009 to start a new organization, Merlin Tuttle’s Bat Conservation.
“He’s an incredible advocate,” says Gary McCracken, a bat researcher and professor emeritus at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville, who first met Dr. Tuttle in 1978. Bat colonies are now “seen as a public attribute, and Merlin deserves a huge amount of credit for that.”
Still, 53% of bat species in North America are at moderate to very high risk of extinction over the next 15 years, according to a 2024 study. The major threats, the study says, include changes in weather patterns and land development, and the spread of a disease known as white-nose syndrome.
“We fear most what we understand least, and bats are easily misunderstood,” says Dr. Tuttle. “Until we educate people to value bats, they’re not going to protect them.”
